issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around war-zone trauma appraisals of injustice/accountability and a threat pattern of hypervigilance, startle, and concentration problems. Self-harm to release overwhelming feelings introduces a distinct affect-regulation strategy that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and sits poorly with the formulation, where Maladaptive Strategies has only a modest reciprocal link with Threat and no links from Negative Appraisals. Given the rest of the profile, a more threat-management strategy would be expected; this item feels clinically out of pattern rather than impossible.

vignette: Kwame remembered the dust first. It had coated his throat as he crouched behind a shattered water pump in the northern district, the generator humming its last before the mortar round hit. He had been coordinating a food distribution for a camp of displaced families when the sky cracked open. He watched through a gap in the corrugated metal roof as the aid convoy scattered, vehicles flipping, the organized rows of supply crates burning into black smoke. He survived by pressing himself into the dirt, counting his breaths, certain that moving meant dying. When the silence finally returned, the relief coordinator was gone. No one was held responsible. The camp was just abandoned. Months later, his body kept that same posture. Kwame sat at his desk in a Chicago glass-and-concrete agency, his shoulders locked tight every time a phone rang or a chair scraped the floor. He was superalert, always watching the main doors, the windows, the fire extinguishers. He started at drop shadows, at the sudden ping of a Slack notification, his pulse jumping before his mind caught up. He had come to believe that threat needed no warning, and that his only job was to stay watchful. The office's open layout, meant to foster collaboration, felt like an exposure to a field he hadn't consented to enter. He checked the room's geometry before answering any client call, mapping the distance to the hallway, the height of the ceiling, the position of the elevators. Alongside the watchfulness ran a quieter certainty. Kwame could not rely on himself to act when it counted, to stay steady under fire, to protect what mattered. He saw the reports online, the political statements, the closed investigations, and he was certain that the people responsible had faced no consequences. What happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it. What frightened him most was the feeling that he couldn't rely on himself. The injustice sat heavy in his chest, separate from the jump in his nerves, separate from the way his thoughts sometimes slipped away. He stopped tracing his work back to earlier drafts. When Maya asked about his weekend, he would offer a summary of errands and groceries, his mind already pulling back from the conversation. He avoided the history channel. He changed the subject when colleagues mentioned travel. The memories stayed at a distance, as if they belonged to a man he once knew, and he let them stay there. The habits accumulated over fourteen months. He began arriving at work early to note which windows faced the street and which stairwells had functional locks. During a quarterly pitch, when the building's automated system triggered a test alarm, he slid beneath the conference table while his team filed out. His supervisor pulled him aside, noting the disruption to client relations, and his lead on a major account was reassigned. Maya watched him flinch when she set down a ceramic bowl, watched him stare at the wall until his breathing slowed. He told himself he was untrustworthy in a crisis, a man who froze when it mattered. He never asked for adjustments at the office. He never explained why he needed to sit facing the door. He simply carried the weight of the unfairness, the absence of answers, and the quiet certainty that he could not be relied upon. He walked into the clinic because the exhaustion had finally outpaced the watchfulness. He could no longer navigate the feed, the spreadsheets, the conversations without his heart hammering against his ribs. He did not want to stay jumpy anymore. He did not want to wonder if he could ever trust himself to be present, to be a husband, to do a job without bracing. He was hoping, quietly, that someone might help him put the guard down, even for an hour.
